genre/aacm-en-chicago-avant-garde.text: In May 1965 the pianist Muhal Richard Abrams and a group of musicians on Chicago's South Side founded the Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians, AACM for short. The association organised its own concerts, taught young people from the neighbourhood and encouraged its members to write their own work. The saxophonist Roscoe Mitchell recorded Sound in 1966, with bells, whistles and small percussion alongside wind instruments. His group grew into the Art Ensemble of Chicago, which lived in France from 1969 to 1971 and performed with painted faces under the motto 'Great Black Music – Ancient to the Future'. Anthony Braxton recorded For Alto in 1969, a double album for unaccompanied saxophone. In this music silence, space and tone colour are as important as notes.
genre/aacm-en-chicago-avant-garde.listen: Hear how silences and small sounds are part of the composition.

genre/aboriginal-muziek-en-de-didgeridoo.text: Aboriginal peoples have lived in Australia for more than 50,000 years, and their songs connect land, ancestors and laws; every song belongs to a place and a group. In Arnhem Land, in the north, the sound of the didgeridoo, called yidaki by the Yolŋu, accompanies them: a eucalyptus trunk hollowed out by termites that drones without interruption thanks to circular breathing. Rock paintings show players from at least a thousand years ago. In 1991 the Yolŋu band Yothu Yindi took those sounds into the charts with Treaty.
genre/aboriginal-muziek-en-de-didgeridoo.listen: Alan Maralung sings a wangga song here that, by his own account, he received from a spirit in a dream. Hear how his clapsticks beat the time and the didgeridoo beneath holds one continuous, droning note.

genre/acid-house.text: On Acid Tracks (1987) the Chicago group Phuture turned the knobs of a Roland TB-303, a failed bass-line machine, as they played. By turning the filter open and closed, the bass line squeaks, squelches and wails: acid house. The sound crossed the ocean and in England became the music of the first raves.
genre/acid-house.listen: In Acid Tracks, follow how the bass line changes as the filter is opened and closed.

genre/acid-jazz.text: Acid jazz emerged in London in the late 1980s, when DJs such as Gilles Peterson played jazz, soul jazz and jazz-funk for a dancing audience. The name was a joke on acid house, the electronic dance music of the moment. In 1987 Peterson and Eddie Piller founded the label Acid Jazz Records; in 1990 Peterson started Talkin' Loud. Around those labels bands formed that played real instruments in the spirit of the old records: The Brand New Heavies, Galliano, Young Disciples, Incognito and Jamiroquai, whose first single appeared on Acid Jazz in 1992. Characteristic features are funky rhythm sections, horns, Hammond organ and soul vocals. Acid jazz drew fresh attention to old Blue Note and CTI records and laid the foundation for nu jazz. (See Mixtape 5.)
genre/acid-jazz.listen: Hear how the band sounds like an old jazz-funk record, but with the beat of a dance club.

genre/afrobeat.text: Around 1970 Fela Kuti in Lagos blended highlife with jazz and the funk of James Brown: Afrobeat. With his band Africa 70 and the drummer Tony Allen he played long tracks of ten minutes and more, with repeated guitar patterns, horns and a driving rhythm. In his lyrics Fela attacked the Nigerian military government, which earned him arrests and violence. Zombie (1976) is a mocking song about soldiers who follow orders without thinking.
genre/afrobeat.listen: In Zombie, hear how drums, bass and guitars build a long groove before the horns and Fela's voice come in.

genre/afrobeats.text: Afrobeats is the West African pop music of the 2010s: danceable songs with a relaxed rhythm, vocals in English, Pidgin and Yoruba, and influences from dancehall, R&B and hip hop. It is something different from the Afrobeat of Fela Kuti, although the name honours that forerunner. Wizkid, Davido and Burna Boy became global stars; Wizkid sang on Drake's One Dance (2016), and Burna Boy won a Grammy in 2021.
genre/afrobeats.listen: In Essence, hear the slow, swaying rhythm with the light percussion and the vocals that lie relaxed over it.

genre/alternatieve-rock.text: Alongside the stadiums, a rock world of small labels, clubs and university radio grew up in the 1980s: alternative rock, in America college rock. Fewer virtuoso solos, a less polished production and original songs. R.E.M. from Athens, Georgia, became big through university radio; U2 from Dublin grew into a stadium band.
genre/alternatieve-rock.listen: In Sunday Bloody Sunday, hear the military pattern on the snare drum and the violin.

genre/amapiano.text: Amapiano emerged in the mid-2010s in the townships around Pretoria and Johannesburg out of South African house and jazz. Characteristic is the log drum, a deep, rubbery bass that works as a melody, beneath calm piano chords and a slow house beat. In the 2020s amapiano went around the world; Tyla's Water (2023) won a Grammy.
genre/amapiano.listen: In Water, hear the log drum: the deep, rolling bass beneath the slow rhythm and the soft vocals.

genre/ambient-drone-en-nieuw-modernisme.text: After 2000 the focus in many film scores shifted from melody to sound and texture. Jonny Greenwood, guitarist of Radiohead, wrote string music with quarter tones and clusters for There Will Be Blood (2007). The Icelander Jóhann Jóhannsson built threatening, low drones for Sicario (2015) and used processed voices in Arrival (2016). Mica Levi gave Under the Skin (2013) sliding, out-of-tune strings. Hildur Guðnadóttir, also from Iceland, wrote part of the music for Joker (2019) before filming began, with her cello in the leading role, and won an Oscar for it. This movement borrows from ambient, drone and contemporary composed music.
genre/ambient-drone-en-nieuw-modernisme.listen: Notice long, sustained sounds and slowly shifting colours instead of a melody.

genre/americana.text: Americana is an American sound that emerged in the concert hall in the 1930s and entered film via documentaries. In 1936 Virgil Thomson wrote the music for The Plow That Broke the Plains, a government documentary about the Dust Bowl, with hymns, cowboy songs and simple harmonies. Aaron Copland followed with Of Mice and Men (1939) and Our Town (1940). His style consists of open fifths and fourths, clear woodwinds and a calm tempo. In this way he evokes wide landscapes and ordinary people, without the heavy Romantic orchestra of Hollywood. For The Heiress Copland received an Oscar in 1950. Westerns and later film composers took over this sound.
genre/americana.listen: Notice the open, empty harmonies and the simple, song-like melodies in the winds and strings.

genre/amerikaanse-indiefilm.text: From the 1980s an independent American cinema with small budgets grew up in New York and around the Sundance festival. The music therefore had to be clever and economical. With Blood Simple (1984) Carter Burwell began a long collaboration with the Coen brothers. For Fargo (1996) he adapted a Norwegian folk melody. Angelo Badalamenti gave the films of David Lynch, beginning with Blue Velvet (1986), a dreamy, slow sound of strings and synthesizers. Thomas Newman built the score of American Beauty (1999) from marimbas, tablas and other percussion. Typical features are small ensembles, repetition as in minimal music and an ironic or alienating tone.
genre/amerikaanse-indiefilm.listen: Notice the small line-up and the repeated patterns that set a mood instead of a big theme.

genre/andalusische-muziek.text: In 822 the musician Ziryab came from Baghdad to the court of Córdoba, and according to tradition he laid the foundation there for an Andalusian tradition of its own. The most important form became the nuba: a long suite of sung poems in a single mode, each section of which begins slowly and speeds up. When Muslim rule in Spain ended, refugees took the music with them to North Africa. Orchestras in Fez, Tlemcen, Algiers and Tunis still play it today, with oud, rebab, violin and drums.
genre/andalusische-muziek.listen: In this section of the Nuba al-Hijaz al-Kabir, hear how the orchestra from Fez sings and plays one melody together, without polyphony.

genre/andesmuziek.text: Long before the Spaniards arrived, the peoples of the Andes were already blowing panpipes made of reed, such as the siku and the antara, and under the Incas they sounded at festivals and rituals. Among the Aymara around Lake Titicaca the siku is divided into two halves, ira and arka, and two players blow the melody in turn. The Spaniards brought stringed instruments, from which the small charango developed. El Cóndor Pasa and groups such as Los Kjarkas later made that sound world famous.
genre/andesmuziek.listen: In this recording of panpipe players from Chimo, near Lake Titicaca, hear how the many pipes together form one broad, rustling sound. Can you hear the melody jumping back and forth between players?

genre/anime.text: From the 1970s Japanese animation received series and films of its own with ambitious music. Hiroshi Miyagawa wrote the orchestral music and the theme song for Uchū Senkan Yamato (1974). For Akira (1988) the music collective Geinoh Yamashirogumi made a score with Indonesian gamelan, Japanese Noh chanting and electronics. In Ghost in the Shell (1995) Kenji Kawai combined a choir in Bulgarian singing style on an ancient Japanese text with drums and synthesizers. With her band Seatbelts, Yoko Kanno wrote big band jazz and blues for the series Cowboy Bebop (1998). Anime music is very diverse and often appears as an album in its own right.
genre/anime.listen: Notice the unexpected combinations: gamelan with electronics, ancient folk singing with synthesizers, big band for fast action.

genre/appalachian-folk-mountain-music.text: From the eighteenth century, immigrants from Scotland, England and Ireland brought ballads and dance music to the Appalachians. The fiddle played the jigs and reels from Scotland and Ireland; in the Appalachians these became above all fast breakdowns in two-four time. Alongside it sounded the banjo, which is Afro-American in origin. Songs passed orally from singer to singer: the folk process.
genre/appalachian-folk-mountain-music.listen: In the Irish Swallowtail Jig, one of the roots of this music, hear the two heavy beats per bar, each of them divided in three.

genre/arabische-klassieke-muziek-maqam.text: In Baghdad, founded in 762, a refined musical culture grew up at the court of the Abbasid caliphs around the oud, a pear-shaped, fretless lute. The singer Ibrahim al-Mawsili and his son Ishaq became famous there, and in the tenth century the philosopher Al-Farabi wrote his Great Book of Music. Everything revolves around the maqam: a mode with its own intervals, sometimes smaller than a semitone, and fixed melodic turns. In a taqsim a player improvises freely within one maqam.
genre/arabische-klassieke-muziek-maqam.listen: Hear how Munir Bashir, in this taqsim on the oud without a fixed metre, explores the maqam Rast and keeps returning to the same tonic.

genre/armeense-duduk.text: The duduk is a double-reed wind instrument made of apricot wood. In Armenia it is also called tsiranapogh, apricot pipe. The reed is strikingly large, which gives the warm, slightly husky sound. Usually two duduks play together: one plays the melody, while the other, using circular breathing, sustains a held note, the dam. How old the instrument is is a matter of debate, but it is certainly centuries old. Djivan Gasparyan brought the duduk as far as Hollywood, including in Gladiator.
genre/armeense-duduk.listen: Djivan Gasparyan plays here with two accompanists. First listen to the bottom layer: can you hear the dam, the unbroken held note? How does the melody move above it?

genre/ars-nova.text: Around 1320 the Parisian scholar Philippe de Vitry wrote a treatise entitled Ars nova, new art. The novelty lay in the rhythm: notes could now be divided into two as well as into three, and smaller note values gave the music more movement. Guillaume de Machaut, a canon in Reims, built motets on recurring rhythmic patterns, called isorhythm. His Messe de Nostre Dame is the oldest complete Mass written by a single composer.
genre/ars-nova.listen: In the Kyrie of Machaut's Mass, hear how four voices rub close against one another, with sharp harmonies that resolve again and again into an open final chord.

genre/art-rock.text: The Velvet Underground of Lou Reed and John Cale worked in New York with the artist Andy Warhol, who designed the sleeve with the banana. Cale had worked with the composer La Monte Young on long, sustained tones. The 1967 debut at first sold poorly, but influenced punk, post-punk and alternative rock.
genre/art-rock.listen: In Venus in Furs, hear Cale's electric viola: a drone full of dissonances.

genre/atonaliteit-en-twaalftoonsmuziek.text: In Vienna around 1908 Arnold Schoenberg let go of key altogether: there is no longer a tonic that the music returns to. In Pierrot lunaire (1912) a woman's voice speaks and sings at once poems about a moonstruck clown. Around 1921 Schoenberg devised the twelve-tone method, in which all twelve notes are used in a fixed series before any one returns. His pupils Alban Berg and Anton Webern continued to work with it, Berg even in a moving violin concerto in 1935.
genre/atonaliteit-en-twaalftoonsmuziek.listen: Hear how the singer in Mondestrunken half speaks and half sings, and only touches the pitches briefly.

genre/azerbeidzjaanse-mugham.text: Mugham is the classical modal music of Azerbaijan, related to the Persian dastgah. A singer, the khanende, plays the frame drum daf himself and is accompanied by the tar, a long-necked lute, and the kamancha, a violin-like bowed instrument. Much is improvised on the spot, which is why masters teach it directly to pupils. In the nineteenth century Shusha became the centre, called the conservatory of the Caucasus. Alim Qasimov is the best-known singer today.
genre/azerbeidzjaanse-mugham.listen: Alim Qasimov sings the beginning of the mugham Bayati Shiraz, with Malik Mansurov on the tar. Notice the voice: how quickly it trills and breaks the note in the ornaments, and how the tar answers it.

genre/baile-funk.text: Baile funk, called funk carioca in Brazil, emerged in the late 1980s at the dance parties (bailes) in the favelas of Rio de Janeiro. DJs first played American Miami bass, fast hip hop with the drum machine. In 1989 DJ Marlboro released the album Funk Brasil, with lyrics in Portuguese. In the late 1990s came the tamborzão, a rhythm with drums from the Afro-Brazilian tradition. Cidinho & Doca sang about life in the favela, and later Anitta brought funk into Brazilian pop.
genre/baile-funk.listen: In Rap da Felicidade, hear the thumping drum machine beneath the refrain Eu só quero é ser feliz: I only want to be happy.

genre/balkanbrass.text: In 1831 Prince Miloš Obrenović founded the first military band of Serbia. In the course of the nineteenth century Roma musicians in particular took up trumpets, tubas and horns and played the folk music of the Balkans, with Turkish influences, at weddings, christenings, harvest festivals and funerals. Since 1961 orchestras have competed every year at the Guča trumpet festival. Boban Marković from Serbia and the Romanian Fanfare Ciocărlia brought the sound to stages all over the world.
genre/balkanbrass.listen: Fejat Sejdić was one of the great Roma trumpeters of Guča. Hear how the trumpet leads the melody and the tubas and horns beneath it play the rhythm and the chords.

genre/barbershop.text: Barbershop is singing for four men without instruments: the lead sings the melody, the tenor sings above it, and the baritone and the bass fill out the chord. Around 1900 it was sung in this way above all by Black Americans, in barbershops, on the street and in church, and later jazz musicians also learned harmony from it. The hallmark is the barbershop chord, a seventh chord that sounds so pure it seems to ring. In 1904 the Haydn Quartet had a big hit with it with Sweet Adeline.
genre/barbershop.listen: In Sweet Adeline, hear how four voices together form a single chord and how the long final notes linger while the other voices move around the melody.

genre/bebop.text: In the early 1940s, young jazz musicians played jam sessions at Minton's Playhouse in Harlem after their work in the big bands. There bebop emerged: music for musicians, often at very fast tempos, sometimes above 250 bpm, with rapid chord changes and long solos. Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie were the pioneers; in Paris and Amsterdam it became the music of the artistic set.
genre/bebop.listen: Anthropology is a contrafact: a new melody over the chord changes of I Got Rhythm.

genre/bel-canto-en-italiaanse-opera.text: Bel canto means beautiful singing: in the Italian opera of the early nineteenth century everything revolved around the voice. With Tancredi (1813) Gioachino Rossini fixed the set form of the aria and in 1816 he had a success with Il barbiere di Siviglia. For La Scala in Milan Vincenzo Bellini wrote Norma (1831), full of long, floating melodies. Giuseppe Verdi made opera more dramatic; La donna è mobile from Rigoletto was being sung in the street the morning after the premiere.
genre/bel-canto-en-italiaanse-opera.listen: In Casta diva, hear how Maria Callas spins out one long melody without haste, with small ornaments on the high notes.

genre/berlijnse-techno.text: After the fall of the Wall in 1989 many buildings in East Berlin stood empty. There clubs emerged such as Tresor (1991), in the vault of a former department store, where techno from Detroit and Berlin came together. The Love Parade grew in the 1990s into a street party with hundreds of thousands of visitors, and Berghain (2004) became one of the best-known clubs in the world. Berlin techno is often bare, dark and hypnotic, with long build-ups.
genre/berlijnse-techno.listen: In Sky and Sand, hear the long, slow build-up above a tight beat, the sound of a Berlin night.

genre/bhangra.text: Bhangra is originally a harvest dance from the Punjab, with the deep strokes of the dhol, a large drum. In the 1980s British-Asian bands in Birmingham and London turned it into modern dance music, with synthesizers and drum machines. Panjabi MC combined bhangra with hip hop: Mundian To Bach Ke became a hit across Europe in 2002.
genre/bhangra.listen: In Mundian To Bach Ke, hear the dhol rhythms and the Punjabi vocals above a hip hop beat with the bass line from Knight Rider.

genre/big-beat.text: Big beat combined the breakbeats of hip hop with rock guitars, samples and the sound of the rave. The Chemical Brothers, The Prodigy and Fatboy Slim from Brighton scored big hits with it in the late 1990s, such as The Rockafeller Skank (1998).
genre/big-beat.listen: In The Rockafeller Skank, hear how a single sampled phrase and a guitar riff are repeated again and again above a heavy breakbeat.

genre/bigband.text: A big band usually numbers twelve to eighteen musicians in fixed sections: trumpets, trombones, saxophones and a rhythm section of piano, guitar, bass and drums. The sections play against one another, often in question-and-answer form, and between them soloists are given room. The arranger writes out who plays what and is therefore almost as important as the bandleader. Fletcher Henderson and Don Redman laid the foundation in New York in the 1920s; Duke Ellington wrote for the personal sound of his own musicians. After the Second World War large orchestras became too expensive, but the form survived: Woody Herman, Stan Kenton, Count Basie, the Thad Jones/Mel Lewis Orchestra, which played every Monday at the Village Vanguard from 1966, and today Maria Schneider. In Europe there are radio orchestras such as the Metropole Orkest from Hilversum.
genre/bigband.listen: Hear how the saxophones and the brass take turns and answer one another.

genre/blaxploitation-soul-en-funk.text: In the early 1970s films appeared with Black leading actors, made for an urban Black audience. Melvin Van Peebles made Sweet Sweetback's Baadasssss Song (1971) and wrote the music himself; it was played by the then still unknown Earth, Wind & Fire. Isaac Hayes, a songwriter at the label Stax in Memphis, wrote the music for Shaft that same year. The wah-wah guitar and the continuous sixteenth notes on the hi-hat in the title track became the sound of the genre. Hayes won the Oscar for best song with it, as the first Black composer to do so. Curtis Mayfield gave Super Fly (1972) songs that were critical of drugs. Roy Ayers wrote jazz-funk for Coffy (1973).
genre/blaxploitation-soul-en-funk.listen: Notice the wah-wah guitar, the continuous hi-hat and the horns that sit as accents above the groove.

genre/bluegrass.text: From the 1940s a fast, acoustic variant emerged in country: bluegrass, named after the band of the mandolin player Bill Monroe from Kentucky, the Blue Grass Boys. In 1945 the banjo player Earl Scruggs from North Carolina joined that band. He played with three fingers, in fast patterns of eight notes per bar: the rolls. In 1948 Scruggs and the singer-guitarist Lester Flatt started a band of their own; their Foggy Mountain Breakdown (1949) was later heard in the film Bonnie and Clyde (1967).
genre/bluegrass.listen: In Foggy Mountain Breakdown, listen to the banjo: three fingers, rolls of eight notes per bar, while fiddle and guitar hold the tempo.

genre/bluesrock.text: Cream, the trio of Eric Clapton, Jack Bruce and Ginger Baker, took the blues to the big halls, with long solos and loud amplifiers; Clapton played Robert Johnson's Cross Road Blues as Crossroads. Janis Joplin also sang blues with loud, screaming rock guitars. Blues rock became the basis of the hard rock of the 1970s.
genre/bluesrock.listen: In White Room, hear the intro in five-four time and the wah-wah pedal that makes the guitar 'talk'.

genre/boerenrock.text: Normaal was founded in 1975 in the Achterhoek around the singer Bennie Jolink and sang in the Achterhoek dialect. Oerend hard (1977) is about two drunken motorcyclists who ride home far too fast after a motocross event, with an accident as the result. The band performed in farmers' smocks and wooden clogs; this music became known as boerenrock, farmers' rock.
genre/boerenrock.listen: Set Oerend hard beside Golden Earring's Radar Love: two rock songs about the road that nobody would confuse with each other.

genre/bollywood-pop-en-disco-r-d-burman-.text: Rahul Dev Burman, son of the composer S.D. Burman, changed the sound of the Hindi film in the late 1960s. He brought in rock, jazz, Latin, funk and later disco and experimented with unusual sounds and effects. Teesri Manzil (1966) was his breakthrough. ‘Dum Maro Dum’ from Hare Rama Hare Krishna (1971), sung by Asha Bhosle, refers to hippie culture. For Sholay (1975) Burman himself sang the dance number ‘Mehbooba Mehbooba’. In the 1980s Bappi Lahiri made disco with synthesizers popular, as in Disco Dancer (1982), which was also very successful in the Soviet Union.
genre/bollywood-pop-en-disco-r-d-burman-.listen: Notice electric guitar, organ, horns and effects sounding alongside Indian instruments and vocals.

genre/bond-en-spionagesound.text: In 1962 Dr. No was given a guitar riff as its signature tune: the James Bond Theme, credited to Monty Norman and arranged by John Barry. Barry then became the regular composer of the series. He combined big brass chords, jazzy horns and electric guitar with a strong title song, such as ‘Goldfinger’ (1964), sung by Shirley Bassey. For The Ipcress File (1965) he used a cimbalom, a Hungarian hammered dulcimer, for a cool spy sound. In On Her Majesty's Secret Service (1969) he deployed a Moog synthesizer. From 1997 David Arnold continued this style in the Bond films, including Casino Royale (2006).
genre/bond-en-spionagesound.listen: Notice the twang guitar, the big brass stabs and the tense, unresolved final chords.

genre/boogie-woogie.text: Boogie-woogie is a piano style from the blues, played in bars and at house parties in the South and later in Chicago. The left hand plays a fast, repeated bass pattern of eight notes per bar, the right hand riffs and blue notes. Pine Top Smith recorded Pine Top's Boogie Woogie in 1928; in the late 1930s the style became a craze, and the rolling left hand returned in rhythm and blues and rock 'n' roll.
genre/boogie-woogie.listen: In Pine Top's Boogie Woogie, hear the left hand playing the same rolling bass pattern again and again, while Smith calls out the dance steps.

genre/bossa-nova.text: In Rio de Janeiro, from 1958 the guitarist and singer João Gilberto and the composer Antônio Carlos Jobim created bossa nova: a soft, restrained version of the samba, with jazz chords and a singing voice that almost whispers. Bossa nova is Brazilian and not Afro-Cuban; the rhythm is different and so is the mood. Through the American saxophonist Stan Getz the style became popular in the United States: Getz/Gilberto (1964), with The Girl from Ipanema sung by Astrud Gilberto, became a hit far beyond the jazz audience.
genre/bossa-nova.listen: In The Girl from Ipanema, hear the soft bossa rhythm on the guitar, the jazz chords and the vocals that almost whisper, followed by Stan Getz's saxophone.

genre/boybands-en-girlbands.text: Every decade has its teen idol, with a recognisable face, a simple hook and a production that suits the medium; in the 1990s came the cast boy band and girl group. The Spice Girls were put together in 1994 through auditions after an advertisement, and became a brand. Wannabe was number 1 in England in 1996 and in the United States in 1997.
genre/boybands-en-girlbands.listen: Hear how in Wannabe the voices take turns, so that each member gets a role of her own.

genre/brill-building-en-girlgroups.text: In the late 1950s young songwriting duos worked in small rooms with a piano in and around the Brill Building on Broadway, such as Carole King and Gerry Goffin, and wrote about what concerned teenagers. Will You Love Me Tomorrow by The Shirelles became the first number 1 by a Black girl group in 1961. Many of those songs ended up with the producer Phil Spector. He recorded them at the Gold Star studio in Los Angeles and piled up guitars, pianos, horns and strings into one dense wall of sound: the Wall of Sound, heard in Be My Baby by The Ronettes (1963).
genre/brill-building-en-girlgroups.listen: In Be My Baby, hear the Wall of Sound: instruments playing double and triple, in a lot of reverb.

genre/british-eurobeat-stock-aitken-wate.text: In the mid-1980s a new pop sound emerged in England out of Italo disco and Hi-NRG: British Eurobeat. The producer trio Stock Aitken Waterman worked like a factory: the same studio, the same musicians, only the singers changed. More than a hundred Top 40 hits came out of their studio in London.
genre/british-eurobeat-stock-aitken-wate.listen: In You Spin Me Round, hear the Hi-NRG bass in eighth notes.

genre/britpop.text: Around 1993 British bands deliberately chose a different direction from American grunge: back to the Beatles, The Kinks, The Who and the mods. In August 1995 Blur from London and Oasis from Manchester released a single on the same day. Blur won the battle for first place, Oasis the one for album sales.
genre/britpop.listen: Hear that Don't Look Back in Anger uses the chord sequence of Pachelbel's Canon and that the piano intro quotes Imagine.

genre/britse-beat-en-british-invasion.text: After hundreds of hours in the clubs of Hamburg, The Beatles became the biggest band in Britain in 1963. From 1964 they, The Rolling Stones, The Animals and The Kinks conquered the American charts: the British Invasion. Bands such as The Who belonged to the mods in London.
genre/britse-beat-en-british-invasion.listen: In Please Please Me, hear how George Martin had a slow ballad sped up into a cheerful pop song.

genre/britse-concertcomponisten-denham-e.text: In Britain well-known concert composers wrote for film from the 1930s. The music director Muir Mathieson brought them to Alexander Korda's studios in Denham and later to other studios, such as Ealing. Arthur Bliss made the music for Things to Come (1936); the march from it became a favourite concert piece. For Laurence Olivier's Henry V (1944) William Walton wrote music with old English and French melodies. Ralph Vaughan Williams later used his score for Scott of the Antarctic (1948) for his Sinfonia antartica. Typically, the music could also be heard apart from the film, as a suite, in the concert hall.
genre/britse-concertcomponisten-denham-e.listen: Notice the brass and the broad, English-sounding melodies, and how the music works as an independent orchestral piece.

genre/britse-en-ierse-volksmuziek.text: From the eighteenth century immigrants from Scotland, England and Ireland settled in the Appalachians. They brought ballads, long narrative songs about love, murder and misfortune that were passed from singer to singer, and dance music for the fiddle, such as jigs and reels. In this way songs such as Barbara Allen came to America. That tradition is the basis of Appalachian folk and country, and, via the folk revival, of the singer-songwriters too.
genre/britse-en-ierse-volksmuziek.listen: In Barbara Allen, hear an unaccompanied ballad in which each verse tells a piece of the story.

genre/britse-kostuum-en-literatuurfilm.text: From the mid-1980s British film adaptations of classic novels and plays became an international success. Merchant Ivory made A Room with a View (1985) with arias by Puccini and music by Richard Robbins. Kenneth Branagh filmed Henry V (1989) again, with music by Patrick Doyle. His ‘Non nobis, Domine’ begins with one voice and grows into a large choir with orchestra. For Emma (1996) Rachel Portman wrote light, dancing music and became the first woman to win an Oscar for film music. In Atonement (2007) Dario Marianelli worked the clatter of a typewriter into the score.
genre/britse-kostuum-en-literatuurfilm.listen: Notice the classical-sounding style with piano, strings and choir, and how a sound from the story sometimes becomes part of the rhythm.

genre/bulgaarse-vrouwenzang.text: In Bulgarian villages women have sung for centuries in the fields and at celebrations, with an open sound without vibrato. In regions such as Shopluk and Pirin one voice sings the melody while the others hold a drone: a sustained note that sometimes rubs against the melody at the distance of a second. From 1951 the composer Philip Koutev brought this singing to the stage with his state ensemble. The album Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares (1975) made the choirs world famous.
genre/bulgaarse-vrouwenzang.listen: Kaval Sviri is about the kaval, the shepherds' flute. Listen to how the voices sometimes lie right next to each other. Can you hear those rubbing seconds, and do they sound out of tune to you, or radiant?

genre/byzantijnse-kerkzang.text: In Constantinople, the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire, a church chant of its own in Greek grew up from the sixth century. Romanos the Melodist, who came from Syria, wrote long sung sermons in stanzas there, called kontakia. Later the melodies were arranged into eight modes, the oktoechos. Instruments do not take part; in the Greek Orthodox Church, where this chant lives on, singers hold a low note beneath the melody, the ison.
genre/byzantijnse-kerkzang.listen: In this Christmas hymn by Romanos, hear how the lead singer ornaments the melody while the others hold one low note.

genre/ca-tru.text: Ca trù is sung poetry from the north of Vietnam. It arose at court and from the fifteenth century spread to inns, village halls and the homes of scholars. The female singer herself taps the rhythm with sticks on a bamboo board, the phách. A man accompanies her on the đàn đáy, a three-stringed long-necked lute, and a connoisseur gives his judgement on the trống chầu, a small drum. After 1945 the art almost disappeared.
genre/ca-tru.listen: Quách Thị Hồ, the singer who helped keep ca trù alive after 1945, sings a hát nói here with lute and drum, the most important form. Can you hear the dry taps of the phách beneath her voice? And when does the listener's drum sound?

genre/calypso.text: Calypso comes from Trinidad, where singers at carnival commented on politics and daily life with humour and mockery. From the 1930s calypso was recorded and became known in America as well. In 1948, on arriving in England aboard the ship Empire Windrush, Lord Kitchener sang London Is the Place for Me, which he recorded two years later. Calypso influenced the music of the entire Caribbean, including that of Jamaica.
genre/calypso.listen: In London Is the Place for Me, hear how the singing almost talks, with lyrics full of detail and a swinging band beneath.

genre/cantu-a-tenore.text: In the villages of Barbagia, in the interior of Sardinia, four men sing the centuries-old cantu a tenore in a small circle. The soloist, the boche, sings the text: epic, satirical or love poetry. The other three, bassu, contra and mesu boche, sing sounds without words. Bassu and contra use a throat technique with a raw, buzzing sound. According to tradition the bassu imitates a cow, the contra a sheep and the mesu boche the wind.
genre/cantu-a-tenore.listen: Tenores di Bitti sing a cantu a ballu, music to dance to. Listen to the low voices beneath the soloist: what does the raw throat sound of the bassu sound like, and can you hear the contra just above it?

genre/cha-cha-cha.text: The cha-cha-chá is a slower and easier-to-dance offshoot of the mambo, devised by the violinist Enrique Jorrín of the Orquesta América in Havana. La Engañadora (1953) is regarded as the first piece. The name comes from the shuffling of the feet on the three quick steps.
genre/cha-cha-cha.listen: In La Engañadora, count along on the three quick steps at the end of each bar: cha-cha-chá.

genre/chanson.text: The French chanson is the song in which the lyrics are central, sung with a great deal of expression, often with a small orchestra or just a piano or accordion. Édith Piaf became world famous with La vie en rose (1947), and the Belgian Jacques Brel and Charles Aznavour wrote songs in the 1950s and 1960s that were translated all over the world. Scott Walker and David Bowie recorded songs by Brel, and Dutch kleinkunst also looked to the chanson.
genre/chanson.listen: In La vie en rose, hear how Piaf's voice carries the lyrics, with the orchestra in the background.

genre/chicago-blues.text: After the Second World War many Black Americans moved from the South to Chicago, and the blues went with them. Muddy Waters and Howlin' Wolf played it electric, with guitar, harmonica, piano, bass and drums, and recorded for the label Chess. Because a whole band had to change chord at the same time, the 12-bar scheme became the standard. British bands such as The Rolling Stones, named after a song by Muddy Waters, built on it.
genre/chicago-blues.listen: In Hoochie Coochie Man, hear the stop-time riff: the band plays a short figure and falls silent, and in that silence Muddy Waters sings.

genre/chicago-jazz.text: During the Great Migration hundreds of thousands of African Americans moved from the South to cities in the North. In the 1920s Chicago became the centre of jazz. King Oliver played with his Creole Jazz Band at the Lincoln Gardens and in 1923 recorded for the label Gennett the first series of important records by Black New Orleans musicians, with the young Louis Armstrong on second cornet. Between 1925 and 1928 Armstrong made studio recordings with his Hot Five and Hot Seven in which the solo became more important than the ensemble playing. Young white musicians, such as the group around Austin High School and Bix Beiderbecke, listened in and developed their own style, with saxophone, faster tempos and more room for soloists. Around 1930 the centre of gravity shifted to New York.
genre/chicago-jazz.listen: Hear how one player from the ensemble steps forward and the rest briefly step back.

genre/chinese-cinema-hongkong-vijfde-gen.text: Chinese film music developed in several places. In Hong Kong, kung fu films such as Jing wu men (1972) with Bruce Lee combined Western action music with Chinese instruments. In the 1980s Cantopop stars sang the title songs, such as Leslie Cheung with ‘當年情’ for Ying hung boon sik (1986). On the mainland the Fifth Generation of directors, with Chen Kaige and Zhang Yimou, used folk songs from northern China, as in Huang tu di (1984). In In the Mood for Love (2000) Wong Kar-wai had a waltz by the Japanese composer Shigeru Umebayashi return again and again. For Wo hu cang long (2000) Tan Dun wrote a score with the cellist Yo-Yo Ma and won an Oscar.
genre/chinese-cinema-hongkong-vijfde-gen.listen: Notice the strings in three-four time in Umebayashi and the cello that, in Tan Dun, floats like a singing voice above Chinese percussion.

genre/choro.text: Around 1870 the flautist Joaquim Callado in Rio de Janeiro played European dances such as the polka, the waltz and the schottische with a small group of flute, two guitars and a cavaquinho, but in a Brazilian way, with rhythms from the Afro-Brazilian lundu. Only Callado could read music; the others improvised the accompaniment. This is how the choro came about, instrumental music full of virtuoso runs and unexpected turns. Pixinguinha later made an art of it, and choro became a root of samba.
genre/choro.listen: In Um a Zero, Benedito Lacerda plays the melody on flute and Pixinguinha a second line on tenor saxophone. Hear how those two lines converse with each other.

genre/city-pop.text: City pop is the smooth, sunny Japanese pop of the late 1970s and the 1980s, made for a country that was growing rich: influences from American soft rock, funk and disco, with tight session musicians. Tatsuro Yamashita and Mariya Takeuchi were the big names. Around 2017 Takeuchi's Plastic Love (1984) became an internet hit via YouTube, and city pop gained a new, worldwide audience.
genre/city-pop.listen: In Plastic Love, hear the funky bass line, the horns and the cool, clear production.

genre/classic-blues.text: In the 1920s the best-selling blues records were by women. Classic blues is urban blues, sung by female singers from the theatre and the tent shows, with a band of piano, horns and sometimes a banjo. Bessie Smith, the Empress of the Blues, recorded Downhearted Blues in 1923.
genre/classic-blues.listen: Notice the AAB form of the lyrics and how the singer, not the guitarist, is the centre of the recording.

genre/concerto-en-sonate.text: In Rome and Venice the violin grew into the star of music. From 1681 Arcangelo Corelli published sonatas and wrote concerti grossi, in which a small group of soloists alternates with the whole string orchestra. Antonio Vivaldi, violin teacher to the orphan girls of the Ospedale della Pietà in Venice, made the solo concerto fast and spectacular; his Le quattro stagioni appeared in 1725 with poems that explain the music. Their forms were imitated all over Europe, by Bach too.
genre/concerto-en-sonate.listen: Hear how two solo violins and a cello alternate with the full string orchestra, and notice when the group sounds large or small.

genre/congolese-rumba-en-soukous.text: Cuban records of son and rumba were popular in Congo in the 1940s. Musicians in Kinshasa made their own music out of them, with interlocking guitar parts and singing in Lingala: Congolese rumba. In 1960 Le Grand Kallé wrote Indépendance Cha Cha, the song of independence, and Franco led OK Jazz for decades. In the 1980s a faster variant, soukous, became popular across Africa and in Paris.
genre/congolese-rumba-en-soukous.listen: In Indépendance Cha Cha, hear the Cuban rhythms, the guitars and the vocals celebrating Congo's independence.

genre/cool-jazz-en-modale-jazz.text: In 1949 and 1950 Miles Davis recorded with a nonet the sessions that were later called Birth of the Cool, with French horn and tuba alongside the usual horns and arrangements by, among others, Gil Evans. Cool Jazz is soft, with little vibrato and a lot of space. With Kind of Blue (1959) Davis took the step to modal jazz; it became the best-selling jazz album ever.
genre/cool-jazz-en-modale-jazz.listen: In Blue in Green, hear the soft trumpet tone with little vibrato and a lot of space between the notes.

genre/country.text: In the 1920s mountain music became country through radio and the gramophone record. Ralph Peer's recordings in Bristol in 1927, with the Carter Family and Jimmie Rodgers, are regarded as the beginning; the Grand Ole Opry made Nashville the capital of the genre. Hank Williams became the blueprint of the country singer-songwriter.
genre/country.listen: In Lovesick Blues you hear two traditions come together: a Tin Pan Alley song from 1922 and the yodel from country.

genre/countryrock.text: In the late 1960s some rock musicians returned to the roots of American music; in 1968 The Byrds recorded Sweetheart of the Rodeo with Gram Parsons. The Rolling Stones recorded Wild Horses with country influence from Gram Parsons, and Eagles from Los Angeles blended rock with country. Hotel California (1977) ends with two guitars playing a solo together.
genre/countryrock.listen: Listen to the ending of Hotel California, where two guitars play the same solo in harmony.

genre/cumbia.text: Cumbia comes from the Caribbean coast of Colombia, where African drums, indigenous flutes and Spanish song forms came together. In the 1940s and 1950s dance orchestras made popular music of it, with horns and accordion. Cumbia then spread across all of Latin America, with variants of its own in Mexico, Peru and Argentina.
genre/cumbia.listen: In La Pollera Colorá, hear the calm, swaying rhythm with the scraping sound of the guacharaca and the horns.

genre/dancehall.text: In the 1980s dancehall emerged in Jamaica, named after the dance venues where sound systems played. DJs, in Jamaica the artists on the microphone, talk and sing over riddims; from Under Mi Sleng Teng (1985) those riddims were increasingly made digitally. Yellowman and later Shabba Ranks became the stars.
genre/dancehall.listen: In Mr. Loverman, hear Shabba Ranks's deep voice over a digital riddim.

genre/delta-blues.text: Around 1890 the blues grew out of the work songs, hollers and spirituals of the Black population in the rural South, with the Mississippi Delta as an important area. Characteristics are the 12-bar scheme with an AAB text, blue notes and slide guitar. In 1936 and 1937 Robert Johnson recorded 29 songs in all.
genre/delta-blues.listen: In Cross Road Blues, count the bars along: Johnson follows the lyrics and stretches the scheme or moves to the next chord early.

genre/detroit-techno.text: In Belleville near Detroit, Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson grew up with the radio show of The Electrifying Mojo, who played Parliament alongside Kraftwerk. Atkins began Cybotron in 1981 and in 1985, as Model 500, released No UFO's. Derrick May described techno as George Clinton and Kraftwerk together in a lift.
genre/detroit-techno.listen: In Strings of Life, hear the strings and piano from a sampler, and the intro without a bass drum.

genre/dialectpop-en-rock.text: From the 1980s more and more bands sang in their own regional language, not as a joke but to tell, close to home, about the village, the countryside and the family. Rowwen Hèze from America in northern Limburg, founded in 1985 around the singer Jack Poels, blended rock with folk and accordion. In Drenthe, Daniël Lohues sang in Drents dialect with Skik. The boerenrock of Normaal had shown that dialect could draw a large audience; in these bands the lyrics are central and the music often sounds more acoustic and more melancholy.
genre/dialectpop-en-rock.listen: Notice how the dialect colours the sound of the singing, and the accordion and acoustic instruments alongside guitar and drums.

genre/disco.text: Disco emerged around 1970 in New York clubs for Black, Latino and gay patrons, such as The Loft and later the Paradise Garage, where the DJ let records flow seamlessly into one another. The rhythm is four-on-the-floor: a bass drum on every beat, around 120 bpm, with strings and horns above. After Disco Demolition Night in 1979, disco lived on as garage and house.
genre/disco.listen: In Le Freak, hear Nile Rodgers's short 'chucking' chords and Bernard Edwards's bass, which keeps moving.

genre/disco-en-synthpopscore.text: The Italian producer Giorgio Moroder made electronic disco with sequencers in Munich, including for Donna Summer. For Midnight Express (1978) he wrote a score built around ‘Chase’, a pulsing piece; the music won him the Oscar for best original score. After that the combination of synthesizer, drum machine and pop song became the sound of Hollywood in the 1980s. Moroder wrote ‘Call Me’ for American Gigolo (1980) and ‘Flashdance... What a Feeling’ for Flashdance (1983). With ‘Axel F’ for Beverly Hills Cop (1984), the German Harold Faltermeyer made a synthesizer melody that became a worldwide hit. Jan Hammer brought that sound to television in the same year with Miami Vice.
genre/disco-en-synthpopscore.listen: Notice the tight sequencer bass, the drum machine and a melody that sticks in your head at once.

genre/disney-en-klassieke-cartoon-mickey.text: With Steamboat Willie (1928) Walt Disney released a cartoon with synchronized sound. Image and sound were matched to each other in advance, so that every jump had a musical counterpart. This precise imitation of movement is called Mickey Mousing. Carl Stalling wrote the music for The Skeleton Dance (1929) and later worked for more than twenty years at Warner Bros., where he strung together quotations from classical and popular repertoire at high speed. His successor Milt Franklyn adapted music by Wagner for What's Opera, Doc? (1957). Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) made songs the heart of the feature-length animated film. In Fantasia (1940) Disney turned it around: Leopold Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra played concert music and the animators made images to go with it.
genre/disney-en-klassieke-cartoon-mickey.listen: Hear how every movement gets a sound of its own: a glissando for a fall, pizzicato for a creeping step, a cymbal crash for a collision.

genre/disney-renaissance.text: After a period of mixed success, Disney animation found a new form in 1989. The composer Alan Menken and the lyricist Howard Ashman brought the craftsmanship of the Broadway musical. Their songs carry the story forward: an 'I want' song lets us hear what the protagonist longs for, a big ensemble number opens up a new world. The Little Mermaid (1989) uses calypso in 'Under the Sea'. Beauty and the Beast (1991) and Aladdin (1992) follow the same model. Ashman died in 1991, after which Tim Rice, among others, wrote the lyrics. For The Lion King (1994) Elton John and Rice wrote the songs and Hans Zimmer made the score, with South African choral singing by Lebo M. All four films won an Oscar for best score.
genre/disney-renaissance.listen: Follow how a song pushes the story forward: notice the transition from speaking to singing and the orchestra that underlines every turn in the text.

genre/doo-wop.text: Doo-wop is vocal harmony singing from the rhythm and blues of the 1950s. Groups of four or five singers rehearsed on street corners in cities such as New York: a lead singer, with beneath him a little chorus that sings sounds and syllables instead of words. Many doo-wop ballads are in 12/8, with a slow, swaying rhythm. The style left its traces in the girl groups, in the early Beatles and later in the backing vocals of Lauryn Hill.
genre/doo-wop.listen: In Earth Angel, hear the little chorus beneath the lead voice and the swaying rhythm in 12/8, in which every beat is divided in three.

genre/downtempo-lounge-en-chill-out.text: Downtempo is slow, atmospheric electronic music with a beat. In the 1990s clubs had separate chill-out rooms, and in Ibiza Café del Mar played calm records at sunset. The softer varieties of trip hop and nu jazz ended up in cafés and hotels and on compilation albums with names such as lounge or chill-out.
genre/downtempo-lounge-en-chill-out.listen: In La Femme d'Argent, hear the slow groove, the electric piano and the soft synthesizers.

genre/drill.text: Drill emerged around 2011 in Chicago: hard, dark rap about the violence in the neighbourhood, with Chief Keef as the best-known name. In London, from about 2014, young people made a variant of their own, UK drill, with sliding 808 bass lines, a skipping rhythm and lyrics that often led to debate. Drill then spread across the world, to the Netherlands too.
genre/drill.listen: In Love Sosa, hear the menacing synthesizers, the heavy 808 and the repeated, almost chanted lines.

genre/dub.text: Jamaican producers put an instrumental version of the riddim on the B-side of singles. King Tubby and Lee 'Scratch' Perry went further: they removed instruments and let them return, and put reverb and echo on drums, bass and snatches of vocals. That style is called dub and turned the studio into an instrument. The techniques of dub returned in jungle, trip hop and dubstep.
genre/dub.listen: In King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown, hear how instruments disappear and come back, with echo on the drums.

genre/dubstep.text: Dubstep emerged in the early 2000s in South London, around Croydon, from UK garage, jungle and dub: a tempo of around 140 bpm, a rhythm with the snare on the third beat, so that it seems half as fast, and a heavy sub-bass. In America around 2010 Skrillex made dubstep hard and loud, with a distorted wobble bass that itself becomes the melody.
genre/dubstep.listen: In Midnight Request Line, hear the space in the slow rhythm and the deep bass beneath it.

genre/duitse-barok-en-bach.text: In Germany the Italian and French styles came together with Lutheran church music and a strong tradition of organists. Dieterich Buxtehude gave his famous evening concerts in Lübeck, while Johann Pachelbel and Georg Philipp Telemann wrote for church, court and city. In 1723 Johann Sebastian Bach became cantor of the Thomaskirche in Leipzig, where he wrote cantatas Sunday after Sunday, and in 1727 the Matthäus-Passion. In his hands several melodies interweave into one rich whole.
genre/duitse-barok-en-bach.listen: Hear how in the third Brandenburg Concerto three groups of strings keep passing a short motif to one another.

genre/dutch-house.text: Around 2008 Dutch DJs such as Chuckie, Afrojack, Laidback Luke and Hardwell made a kind of house of their own, also called dirty Dutch, after Chuckie's parties. Dutch house has shrill, squealing synthesizer sounds, a heavy bass and Latin American rhythms in the percussion. A track builds up to a drop, the moment at which the beat and the bass burst out again. Afrojack scored in 2010 with Take Over Control, and the sound became a building block of American EDM.
genre/dutch-house.listen: In Take Over Control, hear the high, shrill synthesizer line and how everything briefly falls silent before the heavy bass sets in again.

genre/ecm-geluid.text: ECM, Edition of Contemporary Music, was founded in Munich in 1969 by the producer Manfred Eicher. He recorded many records at Talent Studio in Oslo with the sound engineer Jan Erik Kongshaug. The label acquired a recognisable sound: clear, with a lot of space and reverb, and often calm in tempo. The sleeves, too, with photographs of landscapes and austere lettering, are typical. A Canadian magazine called the music 'the most beautiful sound next to silence', and ECM adopted that as its motto. European musicians such as the Norwegian saxophonist Jan Garbarek and the German bassist Eberhard Weber appeared on ECM, but also Americans such as Keith Jarrett and Pat Metheny. Jarrett's solo improvisation at the Cologne Opera House on 24 January 1975 became the best-selling solo album in jazz.
genre/ecm-geluid.listen: Listen to the space around every note: the reverb is part of the music here.

genre/edm.text: Around 2010 electronic dance music became the big new genre in the United States, under the name EDM. Festivals drew hundreds of thousands of visitors and the DJ became a pop star with a light show of his own. Avicii built Levels on a vocal sample of Etta James, and Martin Garrix made Animals on a laptop in his bedroom.
genre/edm.listen: Hear the build-up and the drop: the moment at which the beat and the bass kick in again.

genre/electro.text: Afrika Bambaataa also played Kraftwerk at his parties in the Bronx. In 1982 he recorded Planet Rock with Arthur Baker and John Robie: the melody from Trans-Europe Express and a rhythm modelled on Kraftwerk's Numbers, programmed on the Roland TR-808. This is how electro came about: cold European synthesizers with an American breakbeat.
genre/electro.listen: Hear the 808: a short, dry snare, a ticking hi-hat and a deep bass drum that rings on for a long time.

genre/electroclash.text: Around 2001 electroclash was a collision between electronic dance music and punk. The DJ Larry Tee coined the name and in October 2001 organised the Electroclash Festival in Williamsburg, a district of Brooklyn in New York. The music borrows the cool synthesizers and drum machines of 1980s synth-pop and electro, with detached, half-spoken vocals. Fischerspooner, Peaches, Miss Kittin & The Hacker and the British band Ladytron were the best-known names. Clothes and show were at least as important as the music.
genre/electroclash.listen: In Emerge, hear the tight drum machine and the synthesizer lines that build up further and further, with vocals that sound cool rather than warm.

genre/elektronische-studio-en-musique-co.text: In 1948 Pierre Schaeffer in Paris made music out of recorded sounds: musique concrète. In 1951 the broadcaster WDR in Cologne set up a studio for electronic music, with oscillators, filters and tape recorders; Karlheinz Stockhausen composed there with scissors and sticky tape. And at Philips in Eindhoven Dick Raaijmakers and Tom Dissevelt worked. Ten years later these tape techniques found their way into pop music.
genre/elektronische-studio-en-musique-co.listen: In Gesang der Jünglinge, hear how a boy's voice fuses with electronic sounds.

genre/emo.text: Emo began in the mid-1980s in Washington, when bands such as Rites of Spring played hardcore with personal, emotional lyrics: emotional hardcore. In the 1990s the style became more melodic. Around 2000 emo became big, with Jimmy Eat World, Dashboard Confessional and My Chemical Romance, and with a youth culture of its own of black hair, skinny trousers and eyeliner.
genre/emo.listen: In The Middle, hear the bright guitars and the vocals that reassure: it will be all right.

genre/ethio-jazz.text: Ethio-jazz is the name that the vibraphonist and arranger Mulatu Astatke gave to his blend of Ethiopian music, jazz and Latin. He studied in London and at Berklee in Boston, played with Latin musicians in New York and returned to Addis Ababa in the late 1960s. There, under Emperor Haile Selassie, a lively scene of clubs, hotel bands and small record labels flourished. Ethiopian music uses pentatonic scales of its own, the qenet, such as tezeta and bati; Mulatu laid those over jazz harmony and Latin American rhythms. After the coup of 1974 a curfew and censorship put an end to the nightlife. From 1997 the French label Buda Musique reissued the old recordings in the series Éthiopiques, and in 2005 the director Jim Jarmusch used Mulatu's music in the film Broken Flowers.
genre/ethio-jazz.listen: Listen to the pentatonic scale in the melody and the jazz chords beneath it.

genre/ethiopische-kerkzang.text: According to Ethiopian tradition, Saint Yared arranged the church chant, the zema, in Aksum in the sixth century into three modes: ge'ez for ordinary days, ezel for Lent and araray for great feasts. He is also said to have devised a notation of his own for it. Trained church singers, the debtera, still sing this centuries-old liturgy in Ge'ez. They are accompanied by the large drum kebero and the sistrum tsenatsel, and keep time with a prayer staff.
genre/ethiopische-kerkzang.listen: Listen in this Halleluja from the Ethiopian Orthodox Eucharistic service, the kidase. Does the melody move in large leaps, or does it circle in small steps around a few notes?

genre/eurodance.text: In the early 1990s eurodance was played on the European continent: a solid house beat, a rapped verse and a sung chorus. Producers in Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany and Italy built short pop songs with it. 2 Unlimited had Dutch faces and Belgian producers; No Limit was number 1 in a large part of Europe in 1993.
genre/eurodance.listen: In No Limit, hear the construction kit: a recurring synth riff, a rapped verse, a chorus of almost nothing but the title and a break.

genre/europese-arthouse-en-auteursscore.text: From the 1980s close-knit duos of auteur directors and regular composers emerged in Europe. Gabriel Yared, born in Lebanon, wrote the music of 37°2 le matin (1986) for Jean-Jacques Beineix. Zbigniew Preisner worked with Krzysztof Kieślowski on Dekalog (1988) and Trois couleurs (1993–1994). In Bleu a fictional choral work, a song for the unification of Europe, plays a leading role in the story. For Theo Angelopoulos, Eleni Karaindrou wrote long, slow melodies for small ensembles. Her music for Mia aioniotita kai mia mera (1998) was released on the label ECM. Characteristic are intimate sounds, repetition and little emphasis on action.
genre/europese-arthouse-en-auteursscore.listen: Notice how one simple theme slowly returns and how the silence between the notes is part of the music.
